content:
Hi all, I'd like to announce a new benchmark for proof synthesis in physics that we've been working on at Axiomatic AI. AxQM is a collection of over 1000 proof synthesis tasks in quantum computing and quantum information, formalising almost 500 theorems, exercises, and examples from the foundational textbook by Nielsen and Chuang. We make public the formalised statements with sorrys, all stated within a custom Lean library of finite-dimensional quantum mechanics. Each task is guaranteed a solution, which we hold privately.

The benchmark repo: https://github.com/Axiomatic-AI/AxQM
main branch contains documentation only
independent and dependency-order branches contain the same benchmark library but with different instructions for running it

Please check out the arXiv paper accompanying the benchmark: https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.05157

Perhaps more exciting is the fact that the formalisation of nearly every formalisable item in the book — statement and proof — was done completely autonomously using a general autoformalisation system we built. It demonstrates that the autoformalisation of physics reasoning at the scale of entire textbooks, is now possible.

In the paper, we discuss some potential errors that can occur in any formalisation of physics. We've taken particular care to prevent such errors in the autoformalisation, but the continuous validation of the semantic accuracy of all 1000+ statements will rely on the vigilance of the whole community. Please do take a look and report any issues on GitHub. We will fix any problems in future updates to the benchmark.

We also welcome any comments or suggestions about the formalisation choices (as much as I can say, since almost all of it is autoformalised), and I'm happy to answer any questions.

Congratulations on the work!

I have some questions after a quick look, will explore in more detail later:

Firstly, with my Physlib maintainer hat on:

  1. Can you comment on the API overlap between AxQM and Physlib (including quantum-info)?
  2. AxQM only imports Mathlib but not Physlib. Are there plans to upstream any content? presumably the API developed will also relevant to integrating quantum-info into Physlib
  3. The paper still states Physlean and mentions quantum-info as a separate entity, which doesn't reflect the current state of affairs

some more personal question:

  1. when you say autonomously, does that mean formalising the whole book in one-shot end-to-end without any supervision? is the main difficulty getting your system to that point?
  2. are the failure modes flagged by the system or revealed after human inspection?

will come back if I have more questions!

Congratulations! This looks like great work.

To play devil's advocate a bit (and I apologies for that — but I think these are questions you'll get time and time again for something like this, so worth asking now):

The benchmark repo: https://github.com/Axiomatic-AI/AxQM
main branch contains documentation only
independent and dependency-order branches contain the same benchmark library but with different instructions for running it

My guess is that Fable 5.1 would pass this benchmark with full marks. If it does, what do we actually learn from that? Do you have results comparing different models on it?

Perhaps more exciting is the fact that the formalisation of nearly every formalisable item in the book — statement and proof — was done completely autonomously using a general autoformalisation system we built. It demonstrates that the autoformalisation of physics reasoning at the scale of entire textbooks, is now possible.

Given e.g.

  1. https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.03298
  2. https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.15770
  3. The massive progress in autoformalisation in Tau-Ceti
  4. The formalisation happening in prove2.me
  5. The formalisation of FLT

it doesn't surprise me at all that we can autoformalise a physics textbook like Nielsen and Chuang. So let me ask it differently: is there anything particularly interesting or useful in the output of this autoformalisation, something that would help us produce the best formalisation possible of Quantum Mechanics + info going forward?

Thanks, Zhikai and Joseph! We did autononously formalise the whole book (at least the formalisable numbered items in the book) in one-shot end-to-end, with zero human prompting on the content. This is to be contrasted with some existing autoformalisation efforts, which still require some periodic human encouragement or direction. The Lean statements of textbook problems you see in AxQM today are exactly what was produced by our autoformaliser, just with all proofs and proof machinery erased. We'll be ready to share some more about the autoformalisation system itself in the future, but for now we want to show what it can produce.

When we started, we wanted to see what level of autonomy we could achieve in autoformalising physics, especially in constructing a library. This means we had to start only from a small foundational core of finite-dimensional quantum mechanics, and ask the system to generate the rest, with Nielsen & Chuang as a target. There are other design considerations for this library which we will share in the future, which require a different choice of formalisation than Physlib (or any of the quantum formalisations out there). The resulting library is therefore quite distinct from the quantum parts of Physlib.

If people are interested in particular results in Nielsen & Chuang and would like them in Physlib, I'm happy to discuss how to re-implement them. But since AxQM has a distinct core library, this would not be a simple upstreaming.

Good catch on PhysLean and QuantumInfo. These will be fixed in an update to arXiv.

The failure modes were collected by human inspection of many autoformalised results, and we put this experience into the development of the system that formalised Nielsen & Chuang.

If you gave Fable unlimited time, it might be able to get full marks on the benchmark. Someone should do this, but that's also not the point of the benchmark. The benchmark score should be interpreted against token cost and time. We recommend setting a time limit of, say, 30 min per task. We're in the process of running AxQM on different models / harnesses, and we'll release those results soon.

It is indeed no longer surprising that humans prompting LLMs can now formalise mathematics textbooks / large proofs. I want to emphasise a few distinctions of our approach. One, the full book really was done completely autonomously, with not even occasional human prompting (more details in the future). Two, with the library design, we are making an attempt to formally distinguish between physics and the underlying mathematics. Notably, the source text straddles the boundary between rigorous mathematics and physics. This is very different from formalising a text that is intended to be fully rigorous, and special care had to be taken to ensure semantic correctness of the fully autoformalised physics. Three, our approach is to formalise a large number of examples and problems about the same subject, rather than aim for one big result. This helps to constrain the accuracy and convenience of the autoformalised library, again without any human prompting. This point is what can help Physlib and even Mathlib refine the library design choices.

There are other design considerations for this library which we will share in the future, which require a different choice of formalisation than Physlib (or any of the quantum formalisations out there).

I would very much appreciate some accounting of what types of design considerations these are! We're actively trying to find a common ground for different applications. :)
